A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HiPRAG work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated appendix material.

before.justification: v1 reports original QA benchmark results, training comparisons, reward ablations, manual detection audits and a qualitative case study.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds judge-robustness experiments, retrieval-count comparisons, runtime profiling and format-reward sensitivity results.

M1.justification: The structured trajectories, search detectors, gated hierarchical reward and Algorithms 1–3 retain the same procedure. Alternative judges are tested as robustness configurations. Clarifications about incomplete steps and ablation implementation do not establish a change to the proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions train on NQ and HotpotQA and evaluate the same seven QA benchmarks using the same Wikipedia retrieval environment. The added studies vary judges, reward weights and measurements within this coverage; MuSiQue is only respelled.

E2.justification: The baseline membership in Tables 1–2 is unchanged, including the format-adapted Search-R1 and β-GRPO variants. Table 12 adds retrieval-count measurements for already compared Search-R1 and β-GRPO. The Qwen3 configurations are judge ablations rather than new competing RAG methods.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends evaluation protocols: Appendix G tests 30B and 4B Qwen3 judges with greedy decoding; Appendix H adds retrieval counts under a controlled Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct + PPO comparison; Appendix I profiles runtime on eight A100 GPUs; Appendix J varies format weight with process weight fixed. These supplement the retained main training setup rather than establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendices G–J investigate dependence on judge capability and labeling errors, actual retrieval frequency, training overhead and format-reward sensitivity. These substantially expand robustness and efficiency analysis beyond v1's existing ablations and audits. The earlier case study is retained as Appendix K.

E5.justification: Appendix G newly states that all four alternative judges use a fixed random seed. Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests; the additional judge-accuracy rows do not establish increased replication.

E6.justification: Tables 7–15 add substantial results, including alternative-judge CEM scores of 64.0% and 63.4%, retrieval-count averages of 2.45/2.15/1.75 for Search-R1/β-GRPO/HiPRAG, and reward-assignment time of 42.03 seconds per 324.55-second training step. Existing summaries also change: 7B GRPO HiPRAG OSR becomes 2.3% instead of 4.3%; 7B PPO baseline/HiPRAG USR values change from 29.0%/33.9% to 33.9%/29.0% in Tables 2 and 6. Main accuracy-table results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The substantive mathematical definitions and reward formulation are retained, with no new theorem, proof or derivation. Changing A(a) to A(T) resolves notation consistency. Equation 3 supplies the standard arithmetic mean for the added retrieval-count metric rather than new mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about hierarchical process rewards, accuracy, retrieval efficiency and generalizability. The headline accuracy values remain 65.4% and 67.2%. Specifying that the over-27% baseline OSR comes from previous work clarifies attribution without changing the core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation and applicability boundaries. Section 3.2 explains why locally correct but incomplete steps escape penalties; Section 5.3 explains conservative behavior under excessive process bonuses. Appendices G and J discuss sensitivity to under-search false negatives and possible reward hacking from excessive format rewards. Appendix I interprets the training-cost tradeoff.

D1.justification: v2 discloses how single-detector ablations exclude the other step type and handle trajectories with no evaluated steps. Appendix I adds veRL/vLLM/FSDP details and explains overlapping regeneration batches with verifier calls. These refine implementation documentation; batching and concurrency were already described in v1, and code/model access information is unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds the Qwen3 technical report for its alternative judges and explicitly identifies R1-Searcher++ and β-GRPO as efficiency-focused baselines. The related-work discussion and principal novelty positioning otherwise remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order are retained. v2 adds targeted explanations, ethics and reproducibility statements, and four analysis appendices; the former Appendices G/H become K/L. It also corrects terminology and updates the publication header, without a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands tabular presentation with judge-performance and agreement tables, a retrieval-count comparison, a runtime breakdown and summary/per-dataset format-weight tables (Tables 7–15). Existing figures are retained, and Table 3 removes a duplicate notation row. The main visual change is the new analytical displays rather than pagination.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful evidence about judge dependence and practical efficiency, improves implementation transparency and resolves several text/table inconsistencies. These strengthen assessment of the unchanged method. The gain is limited by new overgeneralizations: Table 12 shows β-GRPO using fewer searches on two datasets, despite the claim of consistently fewest searches; Table 14 shows lower USR at format weight 0.4 than at the claimed best-efficiency setting of 0.2. Run variability also remains unreported.
